title: An Invitation and Four Hard Questions
overview: Jesus tells a story about a rejected wedding invitation, then answers a series of trick questions from religious leaders until no one dares question him further.

parts.label: The refused wedding feast (vv. 1-10)
parts.note: Guests were invited once and called again when the feast was ready, so refusing and even killing the messengers was a shocking insult; the king likely stands for God, his son for Jesus, the first guests for the leaders opposing him, and the street crowd for outsiders welcomed in. Many link the burned city to Rome's destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, though that is interpretation.

parts.label: The guest without wedding clothes (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Scholars are unsure whether hosts supplied festive clothes, but the man clearly came without honoring the occasion, and his punishment is stark and severe. The point seems to be that accepting the invitation also means responding to it, since many are called but few are chosen.

parts.label: Paying taxes to Caesar (vv. 15-22)
parts.note: The Herodians backed Herod's family, which ruled under Rome, so answering yes would anger people under Roman rule and answering no could be reported as rebellion. The coin bore Caesar's image, and many read Jesus' reply as hinting that people, who bear God's image, belong to God.

parts.label: Marriage and the resurrection (vv. 23-33)
parts.note: The Sadducees, a priestly group who denied life after death, mocked it using the old law that a man should marry his brother's childless widow to carry on the family line. Jesus says resurrected life is not a copy of this one, and that God still calling himself the God of long dead ancestors shows they are alive to him.

parts.label: The greatest commandment (vv. 34-40)
parts.note: The Law contained hundreds of commands, and teachers debated which mattered most. Jesus joins two from the Hebrew scriptures, loving God completely and loving your neighbor as yourself, and says every other command depends on these.

parts.label: Whose son is the Messiah? (vv. 41-46)
parts.note: Psalm 110, believed to be by King David and read as being about the coming Messiah, has David calling him "my Lord," which is odd language for a mere descendant. Christians read this as Jesus hinting that he is far more than a human heir of David.

disagreement: Christians differ on what the wedding clothes stand for: some see a goodness God gives as a gift, others a changed way of living that a guest must bring, and many hold both together.
think: What makes an invitation feel like a true gift, even when it comes with some expectation attached?
